pedagogy.summary: This is a data-handling procedure: children measure a shadow's length and direction at intervals across a day, represent the readings in a graph, and read the pattern off it — shadows are long when the Sun is low (morning/evening), shortest around midday, and the direction sweeps around opposite the Sun — connecting the pattern to the Sun's apparent motion caused by Earth's rotation. The emphasis is on fair measurement, consistent recording and revealing a pattern through a graphical display, not on the causes of seasons.
bestPractices: Take real, repeated measurements of the same object's shadow at set times (a fixed gnomon, same spot) so the data are fair and comparable.
Represent the data in a graph and read the pattern from it — the skill is '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-2]', not just observing shadows.
Draw out both variables: shadow LENGTH (a U-shape over the day, shortest at midday) and DIRECTION (sweeping opposite the Sun).
Connect the pattern back to the Sun's apparent position and Earth's rotation, reinforcing that the Sun appears to move because we turn.
Keep to shadow/day-night/seasonal-star patterns; do NOT teach the causes of seasons (assessment boundary).
Use digital tools or careful hand-plotting so the pattern, not measurement error, dominates.
keyRepresentations: A gnomon/sundial casting a shadow that changes through the day.
A line graph of shadow length vs time of day (the U-shape).
A compass-style plot of shadow direction across the day.
A table of time / length / direction readings feeding the graph.
commonMisconceptions: Shadows stay the same size all day.
A shadow points toward the light source (it points away from it).
Shadow length changes randomly rather than in a predictable daily pattern.
The changing shadow proves the Sun itself moves (rather than the Earth rotating).
This daily shadow pattern is the same thing as the cause of the seasons.

learn.summary: A data-handling procedure for ages 10-11: measure the length and direction of the same object's shadow at set times across a day, record readings systematically, represent them in a graph, and read the daily pattern off it — shadows are long when the Sun is low (morning/evening), shortest around midday, and the direction sweeps around always pointing away from the Sun. The pattern is then connected to the Sun's apparent motion caused by Earth's rotation. Emphasis is on fair measurement, consistent recording, and revealing a pattern through a graphical display. Observe the shadow cast on the ground, never look directly at the Sun, and infer the Sun's direction as opposite the shadow. Do NOT teach the causes of seasons (assessment boundary).

activities.title: Build a shadow logger: measure and graph a shadow across the day
feedback: If only length is recorded, prompt in the moment: 'and which way is it pointing now?' and add a compass-direction column to complete the data, rather than reteaching the concept.

If readings are plotted in the order taken or as a bar chart with no time axis, guide the axis choice: put time on the x-axis and length on the y-axis, plot in time order and join the points so the midday dip appears — scaffold the axis choice, don't reteach shadows.

If the learner says the shadow changes because the Sun itself travels across the sky, address the geocentric idea: fix a lamp and turn a globe to show the Sun's apparent motion is our own rotation, then re-read the graph. When relating direction to the Sun, infer the Sun's position from the shadow (opposite to it) rather than looking toward the Sun.

Probe deeper with: 'Why measure at those particular times rather than all at once?', 'Your graph dips in the middle of the day — what is the Sun doing then?', and 'If you did this again in December, would the graph look the same? What might change?'
activities.rationale: The standard's practice is representing [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-2] shadow length and direction; a hands-on measure-and-graph task lets the learner perform exactly that target skill and read the pattern from data they built rather than from a single picture.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-ESS1-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-2]' — assessment does not include causes of seasons; the practice is representing data in graphical displays (bar graphs, pictographs, pie charts) to reveal patterns.
learnerActions: Work safely outdoors: observe and measure the shadow cast on the GROUND; never look directly at the Sun — its position is found from the shadow, which points away from it.
Stand a fixed gnomon (e.g. an upright stick) in a sunny spot and mark its base so it and the recording paper do not move all day.
At four or more set times across the school day, measure the shadow's LENGTH with a ruler AND its DIRECTION with a compass.
Record each reading in a table with columns for time, length and direction.
Plot a line graph with time on the x-axis and shadow length on the y-axis, placing points in time order and joining them, using a sensible scale.
Also plot or draw the shadow's direction across the day (e.g. a compass-style fan showing how the direction sweeps around).
Read the pattern off your graph: when is the shadow longest? shortest? Which way does it point relative to the Sun?
Explain why the shadow is shortest when the Sun is highest, and link the daily change to the Earth rotating so the Sun appears to move.
activities.intendedInsight: The daily shadow pattern lives in the DATA a learner collects and graphs: a U-shaped length curve (longest morning and late afternoon, shortest around midday) and a direction that always points away from the Sun and sweeps around through the day — a visible consequence of the Sun's changing apparent height as the Earth rotates.

activities.title: Interactive gnomon: scrub the day and watch the graph build
feedback: Draw attention to the midday point: ask what the Sun is doing when the length curve reaches its lowest point.
If the learner expects a random or flat line, replay the day slowly so the predictable long-to-short-to-long change (the U-shape) emerges.
Prompt a comparison: how might this curve differ in a different season? (Note the seasonal cause is out of scope — just that the curve can shift, not why.)
activities.rationale: A dynamic model that repositions the shadow live and builds the plotted points as the Sun moves may make the measurement-to-graph mechanism concrete and let a learner rehearse the pattern quickly; it complements, and does not replace, taking real measurements outdoors.
learnerActions: Use a screen model of a gnomon in the Sun where advancing the time of day (e.g. tapping each hour or dragging a time control) swings the shadow around and stretches or shrinks it as the Sun climbs and sinks.
As each hour's reading is captured, see it drop in as a plotted point building a shadow-length-vs-time curve and a direction fan.
After collecting a day's points, identify the U-shape and confirm the shadow is shortest exactly when the Sun is highest, and always points away from the Sun.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the graph assemble point-by-point from the Sun's changing position makes explicit the link between Sun altitude, shadow length and the time-ordered pattern.

activities.title: Static reference: morning / noon / evening shadows
feedback: Ask the learner to point to which time has the shortest shadow, then work out the Sun's direction as opposite the labelled shadow (the Sun's position is inferred from the shadow, not by looking at it).
Use the diagram to challenge the misconception that a shadow points toward the light source: check which way each labelled shadow points relative to the Sun.
activities.rationale: A fixed diagram is a useful scaffold and reference, but it does not let a learner collect readings or build a graph, which is the procedural core of this topic; treat it as support for, not a substitute for, the measure-and-graph activity.
learnerActions: Study a diagram showing the same object's shadow at morning, midday and evening, with labels revealing each shadow's length and direction.
Describe how length and direction differ between the three times and predict what a full day's graph would look like.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference image helps a learner anticipate the shape of the data (shortest at midday, pointing away from the Sun) before or alongside collecting their own readings.

activities.title: Check and sequence the shadow pattern
feedback: If the sequence or traced curve is flat or random, point back to the collected data and the midday-highest-Sun link.
Confirm correct ordering by checking the shortest length sits around midday, when the Sun is highest (not necessarily exactly 12:00 on the clock).
activities.rationale: Sequencing and curve-tracing checks let a learner demonstrate they can read and reproduce the pattern; these are useful consolidation and assessment tasks rather than a replacement for independently collecting and plotting data.
learnerActions: Trace or sketch the expected length-vs-time curve for a day, placing the lowest point around midday, when the Sun is highest (by the clock this may be closer to 1 pm during summer time).
Put a set of shadow images or lengths in time order from morning to evening.
Match a given time of day to the correct shadow length and direction.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates that the daily shadow pattern is predictable and time-ordered: lengths follow a U-shape and direction sweeps around opposite the Sun.

constraints: Keep to shadow / day-night / seasonal-star patterns; do NOT teach the causes of seasons — this is the stated assessment boundary.
Take real, repeated measurements of the SAME object's shadow at set times with a fixed gnomon and fixed paper so the data are fair and comparable.
Observe and measure the shadow cast on the GROUND; never ask a child to look directly at the Sun — the Sun's direction is inferred from the shadow pointing away from it.
Both variables must be drawn out: shadow LENGTH (U-shape over the day, shortest at midday) and DIRECTION (sweeping around, pointing away from the Sun).

A static diagram and a screen model are scaffolds: they cannot substitute for the procedural core of collecting readings and building a graph, though the screen model can rehearse the measurement-to-graph mechanism.
Recognition, sequencing and matching tasks assess that the pattern is understood but do not by themselves elicit the independent measure-and-record-and-plot procedure.
Use digital tools or careful hand-plotting so the pattern, not measurement error, dominates.
Connect the pattern back to the Sun's apparent position and Earth's rotation; reinforce that the Sun appears to move because the Earth turns.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NGSS 5-ESS1-2 citation supports the teaching practice (representing data graphically to reveal shadow patterns) and the assessment boundary excluding causes of seasons; it does not establish the efficacy of any specific activity proposed here.

The misconception claim (shadows don't change size; shadow points toward rather than away from the light) is marked unverified in the source row; retained as commonly reported, not as established fact.

The 'direct fingerprint of the Earth turning' framing from the original recommendation is retained in softened form: the shadow pattern is consistent with Earth's rotation and the activity attributes apparent Sun motion to rotation, rather than claiming the data alone prove it.

A safe-observation method (read the cast shadow on the ground; do not look directly at the Sun; infer the Sun's direction as opposite the shadow) was added to the outdoor activity, the diagram feedback and the constraints; it was implicit in the original but not stated.

probeDeeper: Why did you measure at those particular times rather than all at once?
Your graph dips in the middle of the day — what is the Sun doing then?
If you did this again in December, would the graph look the same? What might change?
assess.correctAnswer: The child measures shadow length AND direction at spaced times, records them systematically in a table, and plots a graph (time on one axis, length on the other) with points in time order and a sensible scale, so the pattern — long shadows morning and late afternoon, shortest around midday — emerges; ideally linking that pattern to the Sun's changing apparent height as the Earth rotates.

errorPatterns.pattern: measures length but never records direction — incomplete data capture
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold in the moment — 'and which way is it pointing now?'; add a compass-direction column. Do not reteach the concept, just complete the data.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: records only how long the shadow is, never which way it points

errorPatterns.pattern: plots the readings in the order taken or as a bar chart, not against time — so no pattern appears
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put time on the x-axis and length on the y-axis, plot in time order and join the points; then the dip-at-midday pattern becomes visible. Scaffold the axis choice, don't reteach shadows.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: axes don't carry time, or points aren't in time order, and the U-shape never shows

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the shadow moves because the Sun itself travels across the sky' surfaces while explaining the plotted pattern (geocentric)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Sun's apparent motion is our own rotation — fix the lamp, turn the globe; then re-read the graph.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes the shadow pattern to the Sun moving rather than the Earth rotating when connecting graph to cause

responseLevels.gap: Measurements are unsystematic (gnomon or paper shifts, times uneven), records length only, or produces no time-ordered graph.
responseLevels.full: Measures length and direction at comparable intervals, tabulates, plots a correctly-axed, time-ordered graph showing the shortest-at-midday pattern, and links it to the Sun's changing apparent position as the Earth rotates; anticipates a seasonal difference.
responseLevels.partial: Collects length at spaced times and plots a graph, but omits direction, or reads the pattern off the graph without connecting it to the Sun's apparent motion / Earth's rotation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a stick standing upright in the ground (a gnomon), a ruler, a compass and squared paper. Across the school day, measure this shadow at four different times and record each one, then make a graph that shows how the shadow changes through the day. Go ahead and set it up — I'll watch how you measure and plot.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching rather than asking exposes procedural gaps a verbal answer hides: does the child keep the gnomon and paper fixed, measure at comparable intervals, capture direction as well as length, choose axes that reveal the pattern, and plot in time order? A child who can recite 'shadows are shortest at midday' but sets up inconsistently or plots unordered bars shows the procedure isn't secure.
